lede: South Leith has been the standing excuse of this archive. Jean Ward's baptism was out of reach; the parish was not transcribed; there was nothing to be done. It is transcribed, it names both her parents, and it took one search.
fits: South Leith — the parish the family tree has always named, and which this archive has repeatedly reported as untranscribed and therefore untestable.
1754. The tree says 1754. Her burial at Chatham in March 1823 gives her age as 66, which implies about 1756 — a stated age two years adrift, which is ordinary.

Her father was JOSEPH. The first child she and Robert D'Arcy baptised at Portsea, in March 1780, was JOSEPH. Scottish naming custom gave a second son the maternal grandfather's name, and this is what that looks like from the outside.
new: Joseph Ward and Martha Garden are an entire generation this archive did not have, and the first Scots in it with names from a record rather than a tree.
caveat: The index does not give an occupation or a residence, and there is more than one Jean Ward in Midlothian — three marriages are linked to this entry, all in 1777, none of which can be hers, since she married Robert D'Arcy at Portsea in June 1779. The parish, the year and the forename of her eldest son are what carry the identification.

george.head: And George Pitt D'Arcy was in the Peninsula.
george.body: The archive knows George Pitt D'Arcy as “Bt: Major 39th Foot” in the Chatham baptism register of March 1826, and as the officer commanding the 39th detachment aboard the convict ship England a fortnight later. He is in the Peninsular War officers' roll for 1808, in the same regiment — the 39th Foot.
george.means: Sixteen years before the voyage, and a war this archive did not know he had fought. The 39th were at Talavera, Busaco, Albuera, the Pyrenees and Toulouse.

closes: Two of this site's longest-standing “cannot be reached” statements were wrong on the same afternoon. South Leith is indexed. The Berkeley register after 1677 is indexed. In both cases the archive had measured the free sources honestly and then quietly widened the conclusion from “not here” to “not anywhere”.
